stops.name: Felpham garden, the fairy's funeral
stops.campa: Alone one evening in the cottage garden, Blake hears a pleasant sound he cannot at first place, and looking closer sees a procession of small creatures, the size and color of green and grey grasshoppers, carrying a body laid out upon a rose-leaf. They bury it with songs too fine for a human ear to hold entire, and then vanish as if the hedge had simply closed over them. He tells it afterward exactly as he saw it, a fairy's funeral witnessed the way another man might witness a neighbor's, and never troubles to soften the report for a listener's disbelief.
stops.quote: A procession of creatures of the size and colour of green and grey grasshoppers, bearing a body laid out on a rose leaf, which they buried with songs, and then disappeared.
stops.quote_source: Blake's account as recorded in Allan Cunningham, Lives of the Most Eminent British Painters, Sculptors and Architects (1830)

stops.name: Felpham garden, the soldier Scofield
stops.campa: A private soldier named John Scofield, billeted at the Fox Inn, wanders drunk into Blake's garden and refuses to leave when told; words rise, and Blake, no small man and roused past patience, takes him by the collar and elbows and marches him bodily the fifty yards down the lane to the inn where he is quartered, before witnesses enough to matter later. Scofield, humiliated, swears out an information that Blake damned the King and called the soldiers all slaves, a charge of sedition in a year when invasion barges are said to be massing across the Channel and every such word is weighed as treason.

stops.name: Chichester Guildhall, the trial for sedition
stops.campa: Bound over by the Petworth magistrates, Blake stands trial at the Chichester Guildhall, once the great church of the Priory, before a jury in a coastal county thick with troops and invasion fear, on Scofield's charge that he cried down the King and called every soldier a slave. Hayley stands surety and testifies to his character; the case against him is thin and full of holes, and the jury acquits him outright, to applause in the courtroom. He walks free of the charge that could have hanged him, but the fright of it, and the county's suspicion of the visionary in its midst, hastens the Blakes' return to London within the year.

stops.name: South Molton Street, the return to London
stops.campa: Shaken but unbowed by the Felpham ordeal, the Blakes take rooms at 17 South Molton Street, Mayfair, where they will stay eighteen years. Hayley's steady patronage is over, and with it the last regular income Blake will ever again enjoy; he returns instead to jobbing engraving work, illustration commissions that pay little and come seldom, and his own unsold, unread prophetic books. He begins here to write Milton and to expand the vast manuscript of Jerusalem, working now for a public he has almost entirely lost, in a city that has already half-forgotten the young engraver's early promise.

stops.name: South Molton Street, 'And did those feet in ancient time'
stops.campa: In the short preface to Milton, Blake sets down sixteen lines that ask whether the holy Lamb of God was ever seen on England's mountains green, whether Jerusalem was builded here among these dark satanic mills, and vows that he will not cease from mental fight nor let his sword sleep in his hand till a new Jerusalem is built in England's green and pleasant land. Almost unread in his lifetime, the verses will one day be set to music and sung in cathedrals and at the last night of the Proms as the nation's second anthem, its author dead in poverty and obscurity a century before anyone thinks to ask his name.
stops.quote: And did those feet in ancient time / Walk upon England's mountains green? / And was the holy Lamb of God / On England's pleasant pastures seen?
stops.quote_source: Milton, a Poem, Preface (composed c. 1804-1808, etched 1810)

stops.name: Broad Street, the 1809 exhibition
stops.campa: Cheated of a commission to illustrate Chaucer's Canterbury Pilgrims by the dealer Robert Cromek, who hands the subject instead to Stothard, Blake mounts his own rival exhibition above his brother James's hosiery shop at 27 Broad Street, sixteen works only, with a Descriptive Catalogue as much manifesto as guide. The single published notice, in The Examiner, calls the pictures wretched daubs, the catalogue a farrago of nonsense and vanity, and the artist himself an unfortunate lunatic whose harmlessness alone keeps him out of confinement. No pictures sell. Blake will not exhibit publicly again in his lifetime.

stops.name: South Molton Street, Jerusalem completed
stops.campa: After sixteen years of writing and engraving, Blake completes and begins to print copies of Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion, the longest and most fully worked of his illuminated books, one hundred plates telling the fall of Albion, the primeval and universal man in whom England and all mankind are one body, and his slow redemption through the imaginative labor of Los. Blake calls it the grandest poem that this world contains, and offers, at its close, to lead any reader who takes hold of it by a golden string wound into a ball straight in at Heaven's gate, built in Jerusalem's wall.
stops.quote: I give you the end of a golden string; / Only wind it into a ball, / It will lead you in at Heaven's gate, / Built in Jerusalem's wall.

stops.name: South Molton Street, John Linnell
stops.campa: Introduced by the engraver George Cumberland's son, the young landscape painter John Linnell calls on Blake, now over sixty, poor and nearly forgotten, and finds not a broken man but a mind undimmed, still full of designs. Linnell will become the second great patron of Blake's life after Hayley, buying and commissioning steadily through the last years, drawing a circle of young admiring artists around the old visionary's chair, and, by simple faithful payment, keeping Blake and Catherine from real want in the years when almost no one else in London remembers his name.

stops.name: Fountain Court, the Strand, the last home
stops.campa: The Blakes give up South Molton Street for two small rooms at 3 Fountain Court, off the Strand, in the house of Catherine's brother-in-law. It is a poor lodging, but the Thames is close, and the rooms are filled, visitors will remember, with an atmosphere of ease and quiet purpose that has nothing of squalor in it despite the poverty. Here, at a plain table by the window, Blake will do nearly all his last and greatest work, Catherine always within call, mixing colors, stretching paper, guarding the door against callers when the work will not bear interruption.

stops.name: Fountain Court, the engravings for the Book of Job
stops.campa: Linnell commissions a full set of engravings illustrating the Book of Job, and Blake, who has drawn Job's sufferings and restoration in watercolor for patrons before, now cuts twenty-two plates entire: Job and his family in the false comfort of outward piety at the start, the whirlwind and the voice out of it, Job's daughters at the end hearing him tell of the visions he has seen. It is the last complete, finished work of his life, engraved with a controlled clarity that even hostile critics will later have to grant, when almost nothing else of his was yet allowed to be great.

stops.name: Fountain Court, the Divine Comedy watercolours begun
stops.campa: Linnell sets Blake to a hundred and one designs illustrating Dante's Divine Comedy, and Blake, who has never read Italian and works from a borrowed translation, throws himself into Dante's Hell, Purgatory and Paradise as into a country he already half knows: Minos coiling his tail in judgment, the whirlwind of the lustful, Dante and Virgil among the ice. He tells his young friends plainly that Dante saw devils where he himself sees none, that Dante was, for all his genius, a mere politician busied with this world as Milton had been, until old age turned him back at last to the God he had known in childhood.

stops.name: Shoreham, Kent, the young disciples, the Ancients
stops.campa: A small circle of young painters, Samuel Palmer, Edward Calvert, George Richmond and Frederick Tatham among them, gather around the old man in his last years, walking out from London to visit him at Fountain Court and retreating themselves to the secluded valley of Shoreham in Kent, which they come to call, half in joke and half in earnest, their own Eden. They call themselves the Ancients in honor of his unfashionable, antique-loving art, and carry his visionary method of pastoral England, seen double, into their own generation's work long after his own name has been let fall by the wider world.
